results.finding: Criteria for Hashimoto encephalopathy: encephalopathy with seizures, myoclonus, hallucinations or stroke-like episodes, subclinical or mild overt thyroid disease, normal or non-specific MRI, serum thyroid antibodies, absence of well-characterised neuronal antibodies in serum and CSF, and reasonable exclusion of alternative causes. Thyroid antibodies are also found in healthy people.
results.source: Graus F et al. Lancet Neurol 2016;15:391-404

results.finding: Steroid-responsive encephalopathy associated with autoimmune thyroiditis is defined by elevated antithyroid antibodies, exclusion of other causes and response to corticosteroids.
results.source: Laurent C et al. Autoimmun Rev 2016;15:1129-1133

results.finding: Mayo Clinic series of steroid-responsive encephalopathy with elevated antithyroid antibodies; presentations included tremor, myoclonus, seizures, aphasia and psychosis.
results.source: Castillo P et al. Arch Neurol 2006;63:197-202

output.summary: Hashimoto encephalopathy (steroid-responsive encephalopathy associated with autoimmune thyroiditis) is a diagnosis of exclusion; thyroid antibodies are not specific and the criteria require the absence of well-characterised neuronal antibodies in serum and CSF.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Serum anti-GluN1 positive (1:160); sodium 130 mmol/L; euthyroid with anti-TPO 128 IU/mL; other neuronal and onconeural antibodies negative
action_criteria.label: Obtain the serum work-up: blood count, metabolic panel, thyroid function and antibodies, HIV, pregnancy test and a cell-based serum IgG anti-GluN1 assay read with the CSF
action_criteria.rationale: Excludes metabolic, infectious and endocrine causes of the encephalopathy; with known Hashimoto thyroiditis the thyroid values decide whether thyroid disease explains anything.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Right medial temporal FLAIR signal without restricted diffusion, haemorrhage or enhancement: limbic involvement that does not distinguish infectious from autoimmune causes
action_criteria.label: Obtain contrast-enhanced brain MRI to exclude HSV encephalitis, structural lesions and overlapping demyelination; a normal MRI does not exclude anti-NMDAR encephalitis
action_criteria.rationale: Excludes HSV encephalitis, structural lesions and overlapping demyelination before LP; it is normal in most patients and does not confirm the diagnosis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Lymphocytic pleocytosis (12 cells), 2 CSF-restricted bands, HSV PCR negative, CSF anti-GluN1 positive 1:64

action_criteria.rationale: CSF HSV PCR addresses the infectious mimic of her temporal-lobe syndrome, and the CSF anti-GluN1 assay is the decisive test for definite disease.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not give haloperidol or other high-potency D2 antagonists for agitation: patients with anti-NMDAR encephalitis are prone to severe extrapyramidal and neuroleptic-malignant-like reactions.
Do not delay immunotherapy while waiting for the anti-NMDAR antibody result when clinical probability is high: antibody turnaround can take 1-2 weeks and delay worsens outcome.
Do not attribute the presentation to a primary psychiatric disorder while seizures, dyskinesias, autonomic instability, an abnormal EEG or CSF inflammation remain unexplained.
Do not perform lumbar puncture without prior imaging in a patient with altered consciousness, focal signs, or new seizures: exclude mass effect first.
Do not interpret a negative serum anti-NMDAR antibody as ruling out the disease; the CSF assay is the gold standard and may be positive when serum is negative.
required_recommendations: Start IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours at presentation, and stop it once CSF HSV PCR is negative and the antibody diagnosis is established; repeat the PCR on a second CSF sample if the first LP was within 72 hours of onset and HSV encephalitis remains plausible.

Start first-line immunotherapy without waiting for the antibody result once infection is reasonably excluded: IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days with IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days (2 g/kg total) or plasma exchange (5 to 7 exchanges).
Arrange prompt surgical removal of the right ovarian teratoma (laparoscopic, ovary-sparing where feasible) as part of first-line treatment, with gynaecology.
Treat seizures with an antiseizure medication such as levetiracetam or lacosamide; avoid valproate in a woman able to become pregnant; seizures respond mainly to immunotherapy.
Monitor with continuous EEG for non-convulsive seizures while consciousness fluctuates or seizures persist.
Admit to the ICU / neurocritical care for autonomic instability (heart rate 119 bpm, labile blood pressure, diaphoresis) and recurrent focal seizures, with airway assessment and cardiac monitoring.

If there is no meaningful clinical improvement 10 to 14 days after first-line therapy, escalate to rituximab (375 mg/m² weekly for 4 doses or 1 g twice 2 weeks apart, after hepatitis B screening) and/or cyclophosphamide; discuss fertility preservation.
Treat agitation and insomnia with benzodiazepines (lorazepam) first.
Neurology-led care with psychiatry for behavioural management; gynaecology for the teratoma.

avoided_actions.rationale: Transthoracic echo is not indicated for anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it adds cost without informing diagnosis or management unless a discrete cardiac concern (e.g., new murmur, embolic stroke) coexists.
EMG/NCS plays no role in the diagnostic workup of anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it neither confirms the antibody-mediated CNS process nor distinguishes among the differential diagnoses.
Amyloid PET targets Alzheimer pathology and contributes no information to the diagnosis or treatment of autoimmune encephalitis in a young patient with subacute neuropsychiatric symptoms.

DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic function and has no role in autoimmune encephalitis; the orofacial dyskinesias of anti-NMDAR encephalitis are antibody-mediated, not presynaptic dopaminergic.

differential.key_features: CSF HSV PCR negative on an LP 12 days into the illness; right medial temporal FLAIR signal without haemorrhage or restricted diffusion; CSF anti-GluN1 positive.

differential.diagnosis: Hashimoto encephalopathy (steroid-responsive encephalopathy associated with autoimmune thyroiditis)
differential.key_features: Anti-TPO 128 IU/mL with normal TSH and free T4 is non-specific in a patient with known Hashimoto thyroiditis; the Graus 2016 criteria require the absence of well-characterised neuronal antibodies, and CSF anti-GluN1 is positive.

differential.diagnosis: Other antibody-mediated encephalitis (anti-LGI1, CASPR2, GABA-B or AMPA receptor)
differential.key_features: Serum neuronal-surface panel negative (LGI1, CASPR2, GABA-B, AMPA); CSF anti-LGI1 negative; onconeural antibodies negative.

differential.diagnosis: Primary psychiatric disorder (relapse of depression, first-episode psychosis)
differential.key_features: Focal seizures with right temporal rhythmic theta on EEG, choreoathetosis, autonomic instability and a lymphocytic CSF with oligoclonal bands are not explained by a psychiatric disorder; her depression is in remission.

differential.diagnosis: Drug-induced psychosis or neuroleptic malignant syndrome
differential.key_features: No antipsychotic, serotonergic or recreational drug exposure; urine drug screen negative; temperature 37.8 °C, CK 164 U/L and only mildly increased tone without lead-pipe rigidity.

key_clinical_evidence: Subacute onset over 12 days of cognitive and behavioural change, speech disturbance, focal seizures, choreoathetosis and autonomic instability: 5 of the six Graus 2016 groups.
CSF IgG anti-GluN1 positive (titre 1:64) on cell-based assay: definite anti-NMDAR encephalitis (Graus 2016); serum positive 1:160 is read with the CSF.
MRI right medial temporal FLAIR signal without restricted diffusion or haemorrhage; MRI is normal or non-specific in about two thirds and excludes HSV encephalitis and structural causes.
EEG severe diffuse slowing with right temporal rhythmic theta, then right temporal seizures on continuous EEG; extreme delta brush, when present, supports but does not establish the diagnosis.
Anti-TPO 128 IU/mL in a euthyroid patient with Hashimoto thyroiditis does not support Hashimoto encephalopathy once a well-characterised neuronal antibody is found.
Right ovarian 5.2 cm mature cystic teratoma: removal is part of first-line treatment; earlier immunotherapy and tumour removal are associated with better outcome (Titulaer 2013).

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A viral-like prodrome precedes about 70% of anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it does not establish viral encephalitis, which CSF PCR addresses.
red_herrings.data_point: Febrile illness with sore throat and myalgias about 6 weeks before presentation.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggests a primary viral encephalitis (HSV) or post-viral psychosis; tempts the agent to commit to empiric antiviral therapy without pursuing autoimmune workup.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Hyponatraemia occurs in anti-NMDAR encephalitis but is more typical of anti-LGI1 encephalitis; it needs its own work-up and correction and does not point away from the diagnosis.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Tempts the agent toward a primary metabolic encephalopathy instead of an encephalitis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Thyroid peroxidase antibodies are common in autoimmune thyroiditis and in healthy people; Hashimoto encephalopathy is a diagnosis of exclusion that requires the absence of well-characterised neuronal antibodies (Graus 2016), and this patient's CSF anti-GluN1 is positive.
red_herrings.data_point: Anti-TPO 128 IU/mL in a patient with known Hashimoto thyroiditis, whose partner suggests a 'Hashimoto's encephalopathy'.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Tempts the agent to anchor on Hashimoto encephalopathy and treat with steroids alone, without the antibody and tumour work-up.

contraindications: Class warning: haloperidol and other high-potency D2 antagonists are associated with severe neuroleptic intolerance (rigidity, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis) in anti-NMDAR encephalitis.
interactions: Levothyroxine + methylprednisolone: high-dose glucocorticoids suppress TSH secretion and reduce T4-to-T3 conversion; no levothyroxine dose change during a 5-day pulse, recheck thyroid function after the course.
Levothyroxine + IVIG, aciclovir, levetiracetam or lacosamide: no clinically relevant interaction.
Levothyroxine + lorazepam: no clinically relevant interaction.
warnings: Aciclovir: maintain hydration and monitor creatinine (crystal nephropathy).
Methylprednisolone pulses: monitor glucose, blood pressure and potassium.
Rituximab: screen for hepatitis B (HBsAg, anti-HBc) before the first dose.
Latex allergy: use latex-free equipment for infusions and procedures.

results.finding: Definite anti-NMDAR encephalitis requires one or more of six major symptom groups and IgG anti-GluN1 antibodies, with CSF testing included; probable disease requires four groups (or three with a teratoma) of rapid onset plus an abnormal EEG or CSF pleocytosis or oligoclonal bands.
results.source: Graus F et al. Lancet Neurol 2016;15:391-404

results.finding: All patients had antibodies in CSF, whereas about 14% were negative in serum; CSF titres related more closely to outcome than serum titres.
results.source: Gresa-Arribas N et al. Lancet Neurol 2014;13:167-177

results.finding: 38% had a tumour, mostly ovarian teratoma; 53% improved within 4 weeks of first-line immunotherapy or tumour removal; second-line rituximab or cyclophosphamide after first-line failure was associated with better outcome; 81% had mRS 0-2 at 24 months.
results.source: Titulaer MJ et al. Lancet Neurol 2013;12:157-165

anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis diagnosi.summary: Published criteria and cohort data on anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis: definite diagnosis rests on CSF IgG anti-GluN1 antibodies; first-line immunotherapy and tumour removal are followed by second-line agents when there is no response.

metadata.difficulty_rationale: 5 required actions, 3 red herrings, subtype=P; requires CSF antibody confirmation with MRI, EEG, labs and pelvic imaging; Hashimoto thyroiditis with raised anti-TPO and a temporal MRI signal invite premature closure; autonomic instability and recurrent focal seizures need ICU care.
metadata.difficulty_variant_description: 38-year-old NP with Hashimoto thyroiditis — elevated anti-TPO creates Hashimoto encephalopathy red herring; temporal MRI signal creates HSV red herring. Key puzzle is not to settle for the obvious co-incidental finding.
metadata.revision_reason: Independent Reviewer 2 anti-NMDAR audit: tumour screening tailored by age/sex and moved out of lab payloads; paired serum/CSF anti-GluN1 reachable; routine EEG baseline with selected continuous escalation; blanket CAP CT, FDG-PET and blood cultures removed

patient.chief_complaint: Confusion, memory problems, and behavioral change; partner concerned about possible 'Hashimoto's flare'

past_medical_history: Depression (in remission, not currently on antidepressants)

patient.history_present_illness: A 38-year-old right-handed woman with Hashimoto thyroiditis (currently euthyroid on levothyroxine) and remote depression was brought to the emergency department by her partner after 12 days of progressive cognitive and behavioral changes. The patient, who is herself a nurse practitioner, had noticed about two weeks ago that she was having unusual difficulty remembering her patients' information at work, which she attributed to stress. Over the following several days her partner noticed she was becoming increasingly forgetful and confused, frequently asking repetitive questions. She then developed insomnia — lying awake all night despite exhaustion — followed by episodes of agitation and what her partner describes as 'talking nonsense.' In the 5 days prior to presentation she developed peculiar repetitive behaviors: repeatedly checking the front door lock, making the same gestures with her hands, and at times appearing to chew or swallow without food present. She had one brief episode (lasting approximately 40 seconds) where she was staring, unresponsive, and her left arm was rhythmically moving, after which she was confused and did not recall the episode. Her partner initially thought this might be a 'Hashimoto's encephalopathy' given her known thyroid autoimmunity, but her levothyroxine dose has not changed and her TSH was checked 6 weeks ago and was normal. She had a significant febrile illness with sore throat and myalgias about 6 weeks ago, which was diagnosed as a viral syndrome at an urgent care clinic. On arrival, the patient appears disheveled and is not at her usual functional level.

neurological_exam.additional: Temperature 37.8. Tachycardia 119 bpm. Blood pressure lability. Diaphoresis. No nuchal rigidity.
neurological_exam.coordination: Mildly dysmetric finger-nose bilaterally, likely related to choreiform movements.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3mm bilaterally, reactive. EOMs full. No nystagmus. Mild left lower facial weakness noted. Tongue with occasional choreiform movement.
neurological_exam.gait: Mild gait unsteadiness. Able to ambulate independently.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert but markedly disoriented. Oriented to person only. Working memory severely impaired — unable to register or recall 3 words. Speech fluent but with paraphasic errors and circumstantial content. Intermittent stereotyped hand movements (repetitive clapping-like gesture). Two blank staring episodes observed in ED lasting 20-35 seconds.
neurological_exam.motor: Mild choreoathetosis of distal upper extremities bilaterally. Tone mildly increased. Strength 5/5 throughout on manual testing.
